# E6 Baselines and ablations (offline, from the stored forecasts)

Computed from the stored `p_up`, decision mids and outcomes of the two calibration runs (R3
taker, R6 maker). Overlap: consecutive decisions share most of their outcome window (a taker decision every ~5.3 s against a 60 s horizon shares it with about 11 neighbours; the maker scores one decision per changed book, about one every 1-2 s). Sample counts below are decisions, not independent samples; the "windows" column (scored time span / horizon) is a rough count of non-overlapping outcome windows. Longer horizons overlap more.

## Out-of-sample comparison (fit on the first half of each run, scored on the second)

- **Model**: the decider's stored `p_up`.
- **B1 constant 0.5**: Brier 0.25 by construction (no information).
- **B2 running base rate**: the dashboard baseline, running from the start of the run.
- **B3 momentum**: `p_up = 0.5 + k * sign(mid now - mid at least 30 s earlier)`, using the
  run's own decision mids; k fitted by least squares on the first half (clipped to +-0.5).
- **A2 isotonic recalibration** of the model's `p_up`, fitted on the first half. If it fixes
  the score, the problem was calibration; if not, there is no ranking to recalibrate.

Lower is better. The first-half labels at the split overlap the second half by up to one
horizon, a small leak in favour of the fitted rows (B3, A2).

| Run | Horizon | n fit | n test | Model | B1 0.5 | B2 base rate | B3 momentum | A2 recalibrated model |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| R3 | 30 s | 514 | 514 | 0.2625 | 0.2500 | 0.2623 | 0.2451 (k=+0.090) | 0.2859 |
| R3 | 60 s | 604 | 605 | 0.2671 | 0.2500 | 0.2567 | 0.2477 (k=+0.128) | 0.2525 |
| R3 | 300 s | 650 | 651 | 0.2676 | 0.2500 | 0.2722 | 0.2481 (k=+0.073) | 0.2954 |
| R6 | 30 s | 614 | 614 | 0.2432 | 0.2500 | 0.2502 | 0.2367 (k=+0.066) | 0.2358 |
| R6 | 60 s | 800 | 800 | 0.2509 | 0.2500 | 0.2551 | 0.2581 (k=-0.032) | 0.2360 |
| R6 | 300 s | 1108 | 1109 | 0.3178 | 0.2500 | 0.2530 | 0.2493 (k=-0.073) | 0.2728 |

## A1 permutation: does the order of the model's forecasts carry information?

The model's own `p_up` values shuffled against the labels 1000 times (seed 20261014). The
p-value is the share of shuffles that score at least as well as the real order (one-sided).
Shuffling ignores overlap between decisions, so the shuffled spread is too narrow and a small
p-value here overstates the evidence; a large one means the real order scores no better than
random order.

| Run | Horizon | n | Model Brier | Mean shuffled Brier | p-value |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| R3 | 30 s | 1028 | 0.2682 | 0.2739 | 0.025 |
| R3 | 60 s | 1209 | 0.2737 | 0.2774 | 0.088 |
| R3 | 300 s | 1301 | 0.2907 | 0.2913 | 0.398 |
| R6 | 30 s | 1228 | 0.2505 | 0.3025 | 0.001 |
| R6 | 60 s | 1600 | 0.2786 | 0.3093 | 0.001 |
| R6 | 300 s | 2217 | 0.3055 | 0.2988 | 0.958 |

## AUC: does the model rank ups above downs at all?

0.5 means no ranking skill. The interval is the same moving-block bootstrap as in E5
(2000 resamples, seed 20261014); the blocks column is decisions / block length.

| Run | Horizon | n | Blocks | AUC | 95% block bootstrap | AUC second half |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| R3 | 30 s | 1028 | 171 | 0.549 | [0.480, 0.612] | 0.536 |
| R3 | 60 s | 1209 | 101 | 0.546 | [0.470, 0.630] | 0.555 |
| R3 | 300 s | 1301 | 23 | 0.525 | [0.421, 0.638] | 0.562 |
| R6 | 30 s | 1228 | 41 | 0.686 | [0.572, 0.793] | 0.734 |
| R6 | 60 s | 1600 | 27 | 0.647 | [0.509, 0.776] | 0.716 |
| R6 | 300 s | 2217 | 7 | 0.503 | [0.395, 0.660] | 0.475 |

AUC interval above 0.5 (with at least 10 blocks): R6 30 s (0.686), R6 60 s (0.647).

What this does and does not show: where the AUC interval sits above 0.5, the model's forecasts ordered ups above downs better than chance in that run, even though its Brier was no better than the base rate (its probabilities leaned down; see E5), and recalibrating them on the first half did not give an interval below the base rate on the second. R6 is one hour (about 58 non-overlapping 60 s windows) on testnet, and this analysis was chosen after seeing the run-level Brier results. It is a lead to test on new runs, not a demonstrated edge. It does not say where the ordering comes from; short-lived effects of a thin testnet book are one possibility not examined here.

## A3 gate sweep (R3 taker only)

For each gate: the decisions that would have traded (`p_up >= gate` buys, `p_up <= 1 - gate`
sells), their Brier, hit rate (the side matched the label) and share of up labels. Gate 0.50
is every decision (side by `p_up >= 0.5`). The bot traded at 0.60, with exits at 60 s; the
hit rate needs reading against the up-label share, since a run of mostly sells in a falling
market hits often without skill.

At the trading horizon (60 s) the would-be trades are not better
than the rest: Brier
0.2737 for every decision, 0.2792 at the bot's gate 0.60
(hit rate 48.7%, n=762) and 0.3096 at
0.70 (n=42).

Limitation: there are no seeds to repeat. The decider is served deterministically and the
runs are on live markets, so a repeat is new data, not a reseed; each run is one sample of
market conditions.
